Scaling and long-reasoning traces (e.g., in o3-Mini or DeepSeek-R1) do not bridge the latent state persistence gap; the underlying latent persistence remains absent.
LLMs exhibit human-centric priors such as the 'Blue-Seven' phenomenon, indicating reliance on stochastic priors rather than committed internal states.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning abilities, we demonstrate that they lack a fundamental aspect of human cognition: working memory. Human working memory is an active cognitive system that enables not only the temporary storage of information but also its processing and utilization, enabling coherent reasoning and decision-making. Without working memory, individuals may produce unrealistic responses, exhibit self-contradictions, and struggle with tasks that require mental reasoning. Existing evaluations using N-back or context-dependent tasks fall short as they allow LLMs to exploit external context rather than retaining the reasoning process in the latent space. We introduce three novel tasks: (1) Number Guessing, (2) Yes-No Deduction, and (3) Math Magic, designed to isolate internal representation from external context. Across seventeen frontier models spanning four major model families, we consistently observe irrational or contradictory behaviors, indicating LLMs' inability to retain and manipulate latent information. Our work establishes a new benchmark for evaluating working memory in LLMs and highlights this limitation as a key bottleneck for advancing reliable reasoning systems. Code and prompts for the experiments are available at https://github.com/penguinnnnn/LLM-Working-Memory.

papers.title: Comprehension Without Competence: Architectural Limits of LLMs in Symbolic Computation and Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do Large Language Models (LLMs) systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency, despite being able to fluently explain the correct principles?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and analyzes a fundamental architectural limitation in LLMs termed the 'computational split-brain syndrome,' where models can explain principles they cannot reliably execute, due to geometric separation of instruction and execution pathways.
papers.conclusion: LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning, and fundamental architectural innovations are needed to overcome these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a systematic gap between comprehension (explaining principles) and competence (executing them), termed computational split-brain syndrome.
This gap is rooted in architectural constraints: token embeddings resist domain binding, FFNs cannot implement exact symbolic operations, and next-token prediction decouples instruction from execution.
The syndrome manifests across domains (arithmetic and relational reasoning) and is not resolved by scaling or prompting.
Compensatory strategies (self-scaffolding, tool delegation, hybrid architectures) are necessary but highlight the need for metacognitive capabilities that current architectures lack.
Mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles.
papers.limitation:
Focus on pretrained transformer-based LLMs without external tools or explicit reasoning scaffolds.
Empirical evaluation centers on specific model families (LLaMA2, Claude, GPT-4) and may not generalize to fundamentally different architectures.
Geometric separation experiments rely on t-SNE projections which may not capture all relevant representational structure.
Theoretical analysis of FFN computational limits focuses on ReLU networks and may not apply to other activation functions.
future_direction: Developing future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution.
Empirical validation of the hypothesis that similar constraints apply to architectural variations like mixture-of-experts.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) display striking surface fluency yet systematically fail at tasks requiring symbolic reasoning, arithmetic accuracy, and logical consistency. This paper offers a structural diagnosis of such failures, revealing a persistent gap between \textit{comprehension} and \textit{competence}. Through controlled experiments and architectural analysis, we demonstrate that LLMs often articulate correct principles without reliably applying them--a failure rooted not in knowledge access, but in computational execution. We term this phenomenon the computational \textit{split-brain syndrome}, where instruction and action pathways are geometrically and functionally dissociated. This core limitation recurs across domains, from mathematical operations to relational inferences, and explains why model behavior remains brittle even under idealized prompting. We argue that LLMs function as powerful pattern completion engines, but lack the architectural scaffolding for principled, compositional reasoning. Our findings delineate the boundary of current LLM capabilities and motivate future models with metacognitive control, principle lifting, and structurally grounded execution. This diagnosis also clarifies why mechanistic interpretability findings may reflect training-specific pattern coordination rather than universal computational principles, and why the geometric separation between instruction and execution pathways suggests limitations in neural introspection and mechanistic analysis.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations in Base 10
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent numbers? Specifically, do they use digit-wise representations in base 10 rather than a linear value space?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally represent numbers using individual circular representations per-digit in base 10, which explains their error patterns on numerical tasks.
papers.conclusion: Circular digit-wise probes can effectively extract number representations in base 10, and editing these representations can alter model generation, suggesting digit-wise representations are used for arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
LLM errors on numerical tasks are often scattered across the digits of the answer rather than normally distributed around its numeric value.
Probes can accurately recover digit values in base 10 from hidden representations, but not the whole number value directly.
Causal interventions on digit representations can modify the number accordingly, confirming the causal significance of digit-wise representations.
The digit-wise representation is base-10 specific, with high accuracy for base 10 probes compared to other bases.
This representation holds across models with different tokenization schemes, such as Llama 3 8B and Mistral 7B.
papers.limitation:
The study does not conclusively show that digit-wise representation is the only representation of numeracy in LLMs; there may be superposition of multiple redundant representations.
The focus is exclusively on natural numbers, leaving fractions and other numeric values for future work.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to fractions and other numeric values beyond natural numbers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently make errors when handling even simple numerical problems, such as comparing two small numbers. A natural hypothesis is that these errors stem from how LLMs represent numbers, and specifically, whether their representations of numbers capture their numeric values. We tackle this question from the observation that LLM errors on numerical tasks are often distributed across the digits of the answer rather than normally around its numeric value. Through a series of probing experiments and causal interventions, we show that LLMs internally represent numbers with individual circular representations per-digit in base 10. This digit-wise representation, as opposed to a value representation, sheds light on the error patterns of models on tasks involving numerical reasoning and could serve as a basis for future studies on analyzing numerical mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: Deciphering the Factors Influencing the Efficacy of Chain-of-Thought: Probability, Memorization, and Noisy Reasoning
papers.research_question: What factors influence the efficacy of Chain-of-Thought prompting in Large Language Models? Specifically, does CoT performance reflect abstract reasoning or shallow heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting performance in LLMs is influenced by three factors: the probability of the correct output, memorization of frequent patterns from pre-training, and noisy reasoning where error rate increases with task difficulty.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning, supporting a middle-ground viewpoint in the debate about LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
CoT performance is affected by the probability of the correct output, with higher probability outputs leading to higher accuracy.
Memorization plays a role, as evidenced by a spike in accuracy for shift level 13 (rot-13), which is common in internet text and training data.
Noisy reasoning is observed: accuracy decreases as the number of implicit reasoning steps (shift level) increases, indicating a noisy reasoning process.
Unfaithfulness between intermediate reasoning steps and the final answer occurs, especially for low-probability outputs, where the model may 'self-correct' to a higher-probability word.
CoT can be effective even when the demonstration in the prompt is invalid, suggesting the format of reasoning steps is more important than their correctness.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to enhance the multi-step reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, debates persist about whether LLMs exhibit abstract generalization or rely on shallow heuristics when given CoT prompts. To understand the factors influencing CoT reasoning we provide a detailed case study of the symbolic reasoning task of decoding shift ciphers, where letters are shifted forward some number of steps in the alphabet. We analyze the pattern of results produced by three LLMs -- GPT-4, Claude 3, and Llama 3.1 -- performing this task using CoT prompting. By focusing on a single relatively simple task, we are able to identify three factors that systematically affect CoT performance: the probability of the task's expected output (probability), what the model has implicitly learned during pre-training (memorization), and the number of intermediate operations involved in reasoning (noisy reasoning). We show that these factors can drastically influence task accuracy across all three LLMs; e.g., when tested with GPT-4, varying the output's probability of occurrence shifts accuracy from 26% to 70%. Overall, we conclude that CoT prompting performance reflects both memorization and a probabilistic version of genuine reasoning. Code and data at this https://github.com/aksh555/deciphering_cot

papers.title: A Language Model with Limited Memory Capacity Captures Interference in Human Sentence Processing
papers.research_question: Can a neural language model with limited memory capacity capture similarity-based interference effects in human sentence processing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a cue-based retrieval recurrent neural network (CBR-RNN) with a single attention head, demonstrating that it can capture similarity-based interference effects in human sentence processing without hand-picked linguistic features.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that mechanistic explanations of processing difficulty rooted in memory retrieval constraints can emerge as a by-product of minimizing the surprisal of upcoming words.
papers.key_findings:
The CBR-RNN's attention mechanism tracks subject-verb dependencies over long distances and with intervening nouns.
The model captures both semantic and syntactic interference effects in agreement attraction experiments.
Surprisal estimates from the model predict human plausibility ratings for attraction effects.
Relative attention from the single head shows additive effects of semantic and agreement attraction in double violations.
GPT-2's attention heads exhibit complementary interference effects, highlighting challenges in aggregating multiple heads.
papers.limitation:
Limited to subject-verb dependencies, not other dependency types.
Assumptions about working memory differ from cue-based theories, e.g., items are timestep representations not syntactic constituents.
It is unclear if the model learns interpretable linguistic features like [+/-subject].
Training data is from Wikipedia, not developmentally plausible like child-directed speech.
future_direction: Evaluate on various dependency types like reflexive anaphora and filler-gap dependencies.
Incorporate syntactic attention masking or memory decay mechanisms.
Use causal representational probing to interpret learned features.
papers.abstract: Two of the central factors believed to underpin human sentence processing difficulty are expectations and retrieval from working memory. A recent attempt to create a unified cognitive model integrating these two factors relied on the parallels between the self-attention mechanism of transformer language models and cue-based retrieval theories of working memory in human sentence processing (Ryu and Lewis 2021). While Ryu and Lewis show that attention patterns in specialized attention heads of GPT-2 are consistent with similarity-based interference, a key prediction of cue-based retrieval models, their method requires identifying syntactically specialized attention heads, and makes the cognitively implausible assumption that hundreds of memory retrieval operations take place in parallel. In the present work, we develop a recurrent neural language model with a single self-attention head, which more closely parallels the memory system assumed by cognitive theories. We show that our model's single attention head captures semantic and syntactic interference effects observed in human experiments.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Chain-of-Thought: A Latent Computational Mode in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of Chain-of-Thought prompting in triggering reasoning in large language models? Is CoT the unique mechanism or just one of several triggers for a latent reasoning capability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning in LLMs can be triggered by steering latent internal features identified via Sparse Autoencoders, indicating that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not the unique pathway but one of several triggers for an underlying reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in large language models can be triggered by activating latent internal features, showing that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not unique and that activation-level interventions are useful for understanding and controlling reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single reasoning-related latent feature improves reasoning accuracy without explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Early single-feature steering leads to more concise reasoning outputs in large models, matching or exceeding CoT performance with fewer tokens.
The identified reasoning feature is activated early in generation and is associated with entering a reasoning mode rather than predicting answer correctness.
The reasoning feature generalizes across different prompts that encourage reasoning (e.g., 'Explain how', 'Solve carefully'), not just step-by-step prompts.
Random feature steering does not produce similar improvements, confirming the specificity of the identified reasoning-related feature.
papers.limitation: The identified SAE features are not fully disentangled or isolated reasoning mechanisms; conclusions are based on behavioral and intervention-level evidence, not complete mechanistic characterization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear why it works and whether it is the unique mechanism for triggering reasoning in large language models. In this work, we study this question by directly analyzing and intervening on the internal representations of LLMs with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), identifying a small set of latent features that are causally associated with LLM reasoning behavior. Across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks, we find that steering a single reasoning-related latent feature can substantially improve accuracy without explicit CoT prompting. For large models, latent steering achieves performance comparable to standard CoT prompting while producing more efficient outputs. We further observe that this reasoning-oriented internal state is triggered early in generation and can override prompt-level instructions that discourage explicit reasoning. Overall, our results suggest that multi-step reasoning in LLMs is supported by latent internal activations that can be externally activated, while CoT prompting is one effective, but not unique, way of activating this mechanism rather than its necessary cause.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between looping and depth-growing in LLMs, and do they share a common mechanism for improving reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper unifies looping and depth-growing in LLMs, showing they share mechanistic signatures of iterative computation and can be composed to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Depth growing and looping are complementary methods for inducing iterative computation to improve reasoning, and their unification suggests a simple reasoning recipe.
papers.key_findings:
Looped and depth-grown models exhibit similar depth-wise computational signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and periodic patterns aligned with the block size.
Depth-grown models can be looped at inference time to improve reasoning performance without being trained to loop.
Looped and depth-grown models adapt better than baselines to in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning.
Depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using high-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures.
The 'grow first, loop later' strategy yields the strongest reasoning performance under matched data and inference FLOPs.
papers.limitation: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models may improve performance, but this is left for future work.
future_direction: Tuning the baseline training hyperparameters for depth-grown or looped models to improve performance.
papers.abstract: Looping, reusing a block of layers across depth, and depth growing, training shallow-to-deep models by duplicating middle layers, have both been linked to stronger reasoning, but their relationship remains unclear. We provide a mechanistic unification: looped and depth-grown models exhibit convergent depth-wise signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and recurring patterns aligned with the looped or grown block. These shared signatures support the view that their gains stem from a common form of iterative computation. Building on this connection, we show that the two techniques are adaptable and composable: applying inference-time looping to the middle blocks of a depth-grown model improves accuracy on some reasoning primitives by up to $2\times$, despite the model never being trained to loop. Both approaches also adapt better than the baseline when given more in-context examples or additional supervised fine-tuning data. Additionally, depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using higher-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures, which can be further boosted by adapting a middle block to loop. Overall, our results position depth growth and looping as complementary, practical methods for inducing and scaling iterative computation to improve reasoning.

papers.title: Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition
papers.research_question: How do large language models compute addition? The paper reverse engineers the mechanism by which LLMs perform addition.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs represent numbers as generalized helices and compute addition by manipulating these helices using the Clock algorithm.
papers.conclusion: LLMs represent numbers as helices and use the interpretable Clock algorithm to compute addition, providing insight into their mathematical capabilities and potential errors.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs represent numbers as a generalized helix with both periodic and linear components.
The helical representation is causally implicated in addition and other arithmetic tasks like subtraction and multiplication.
LLMs use the Clock algorithm to compute addition by rotating the helices representing the addends.
Specific model components (MLPs, attention heads, neurons) implement steps of the Clock algorithm, with MLPs playing a dominant role.
The Clock algorithm is used across multiple mid-sized LLMs (GPT-J, Pythia-6.9B, Llama3.1-8B).
papers.limitation:
The Clock algorithm might be one method in an ensemble of algorithms used by LLMs for addition.
Different tokenization schemes in other models may require modified algorithms, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work could analyze if LLMs have internal error-correcting codes for addition similar to grid cells.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning is an increasingly important indicator of large language model (LLM) capabilities, yet we lack understanding of how LLMs process even simple mathematical tasks. To address this, we reverse engineer how three mid-sized LLMs compute addition. We first discover that numbers are represented in these LLMs as a generalized helix, which is strongly causally implicated for the tasks of addition and subtraction, and is also causally relevant for integer division, multiplication, and modular arithmetic. We then propose that LLMs compute addition by manipulating this generalized helix using the "Clock" algorithm: to solve $a+b$, the helices for $a$ and $b$ are manipulated to produce the $a+b$ answer helix which is then read out to model logits. We model influential MLP outputs, attention head outputs, and even individual neuron preactivations with these helices and verify our understanding with causal interventions. By demonstrating that LLMs represent numbers on a helix and manipulate this helix to perform addition, we present the first representation-level explanation of an LLM's mathematical capability.

papers.title: Unveiling Factual Recall Behaviors of Large Language Models through Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How effectively do Large Language Models retrieve and utilize their internal factual knowledge for multi-hop reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs often fail to retrieve relevant factual knowledge during reasoning; enhancing factual recall improves reasoning performance, while Chain-of-Thought prompting helps by stimulating step-by-step reasoning and reducing shortcuts.
papers.conclusion: Factual recall is crucial for correct reasoning in LLMs; CoT stimulates recall and reduces shortcuts, and contextual conflicts can affect the retrieval process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not consistently retrieve pertinent factual knowledge for reasoning, with more than a third of reasoning errors stemming from deficiencies in retrieval.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting enhances factual recall by facilitating step-by-step reasoning, reducing the likelihood of shortcuts.
Manually enhancing the factual recall process improves reasoning performance, while suppressing it leads to notable degradation.
The presence of knowledge conflict in the context can enhance the retrieval of the corresponding fact during reasoning.
A considerable proportion of correctly answered questions under no CoT setting rely on shortcuts rather than full multi-hop reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability: Findings are based on specific LLMs and the TFRKN dataset; future research should extend to various models and datasets.
Theoretical Analysis: Empirical evidence is provided, but a deeper theoretical analysis is needed to fully comprehend the underlying reasons.
Practical Applications: The paper discusses theoretical aspects but does not delve into practical applications to enhance reasoning capabilities.
future_direction: Extend findings to verify generalizability across various models and datasets.
Conduct deeper theoretical analysis to understand the observed phenomena.
Explore how the findings can be applied in practical scenarios to enhance LLM reasoning capabilities.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) actively recall or retrieve their internal repositories of factual knowledge when faced with reasoning tasks. Through an analysis of LLMs' internal factual recall at each reasoning step via Knowledge Neurons, we reveal that LLMs fail to harness the critical factual associations under certain circumstances. Instead, they tend to opt for alternative, shortcut-like pathways to answer reasoning questions. By manually manipulating the recall process of parametric knowledge in LLMs, we demonstrate that enhancing this recall process directly improves reasoning performance whereas suppressing it leads to notable degradation. Furthermore, we assess the effect of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a powerful technique for addressing complex reasoning tasks. Our findings indicate that CoT can intensify the recall of factual knowledge by encouraging LLMs to engage in orderly and reliable reasoning. Furthermore, we explored how contextual conflicts affect the retrieval of facts during the reasoning process to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factual recall behaviors of LLMs. Code and data will be available soon.

papers.title: Supervised and Unsupervised Probing of Shortcut Learning: Case Study on the Emergence and Evolution of Syntactic Heuristics in BERT
papers.research_question: When and how do syntactic heuristics (shortcuts) emerge and evolve in BERT during fine-tuning, and how do they affect the model's latent knowledge and outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that syntactic heuristics emerge during fine-tuning, vary across layers, and that models retain task-relevant information despite shortcut reliance, using a novel combination of supervised and unsupervised probes.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the progressive adoption of syntactic heuristics with fine-tuning dataset size, observable across hidden layers, and shows that models retain task-relevant information despite shortcut reliance, with supervised and unsupervised probes processing information differently.
papers.key_findings:
Syntactic heuristics are absent in pretrained models but emerge and evolve with increasing fine-tuning dataset size.
The reliance on shortcuts is most pronounced in the final layers (closer to output) but not exclusively output-driven.
Despite shortcut reliance during inference, the model retains relevant information in hidden representations, as shown by supervised probing.
Supervised and unsupervised probes capture different aspects of the model's knowledge, with CCS providing an unsupervised way to access latent knowledge.
Fine-tuning with a mixed dataset (including challenging examples) mitigates shortcut adoption.
papers.limitation:
Focus on BERT, a relatively small model, limiting generalizability to larger or more recent architectures.
Only examined full fine-tuning, not parameter-efficient methods like adapters.
Assessed reliance on shortcuts by considering three heuristics as a whole, not isolating each.
future_direction: Extending the approach to more recent and diverse models to assess robustness of findings.
Investigating parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (e.g., adapters) and their impact on shortcut learning.
Exploring more datasets and heuristics to confirm findings.
papers.abstract: Contemporary language models (LMs) such as BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), T5 (Raffel et al., 2023), GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023), have exhibited remarkable capabilities, effectively addressing long-standing challenges in the field.However, these models rely on shortcut learning, using a decision rule that relies on superficial cues that are spuriously correlated with the labels (Geirhos et al., 2020).In this research, we focus on the reliance on a specific type of shortcuts, namely syntactic heuristics, in BERT when performing Natural Language Inference (NLI), a representative task in Natural Language Understanding (Jeretic et al., 2020).By making use of two probing methods, one supervised, one unsupervised, we investigate where these shortcuts emerge, how they evolve and how they impact the latent knowledge of the LM.Our findings reveal that syntactic heuristics are absent in pretrained models but emerge and evolve as the model is finetuned with datasets of increasing size.The adoption of these shortcuts varies across different hidden layers, with specific layers closer to the output contributing more to this phenomenon.Despite the model's reliance on shortcuts during inference, it retains information relevant to the task, and our supervised and unsupervised probes process this information differently.

papers.title: Debiasing Masks: A New Framework for Shortcut Mitigation in NLU
papers.research_question: How can language models be debiased from shortcut behaviors in NLU tasks by identifying and removing specific weights, without requiring full model retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a new debiasing framework that finds pruning masks to remove biased weights from a fine-tuned model, enabling flexible application and removal of debiasing behaviors without retraining.
papers.conclusion: Debiasing masks are an effective approach to mitigating shortcuts, reframing debiasing as removing specific weights from a network rather than training separate models.
papers.key_findings:
Debiasing masks are effective, matching or surpassing standard debiasing methods on several NLU tasks.
Masks are diverse and can target different biases (e.g., lexical overlap, negation words).
Analysis of generated masks shows higher pruning rates in early layers and attention modules, suggesting these areas may be important for bias encoding.
Pruning alone without a debiasing loss does not achieve the same debiasing effect.
Masks can be stored efficiently and applied/removed at inference time, offering flexibility.
papers.limitation:
The movement pruning technique requires 12 epochs of training, leading to longer training times.
The paper explores only three NLU tasks with a fixed pruning configuration; applicability to other domains and configurations needs further exploration.
future_direction: Reduce the training time required for the mask search approach.
Explore applicability to other domains beyond the three NLU tasks studied.
Combine the masking approach with other debiasing methods.
Explore more varied configurations, such as structured pruning methods for improved inference efficiency.
papers.abstract: Debiasing language models from unwanted behaviors in Natural Language Understanding tasks is a topic with rapidly increasing interest in the NLP community. Spurious statistical correlations in the data allow models to perform shortcuts and avoid uncovering more advanced and desirable linguistic features. A multitude of effective debiasing approaches has been proposed, but flexibility remains a major issue. For the most part, models must be retrained to find a new set of weights with debiased behavior. We propose a new debiasing method in which we identify debiased pruning masks that can be applied to a finetuned model. This enables the selective and conditional application of debiasing behaviors. We assume that bias is caused by a certain subset of weights in the network; our method is, in essence, a mask search to identify and remove biased weights. Our masks show equivalent or superior performance to the standard counterparts, while offering important benefits. Pruning masks can be stored with high efficiency in memory, and it becomes possible to switch among several debiasing behaviors (or revert back to the original biased model) at inference time. Finally, it opens the doors to further research on how biases are acquired by studying the generated masks. For example, we observed that the early layers and attention heads were pruned more aggressively, possibly hinting towards the location in which biases may be encoded.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models learn grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data? What does this consistency reveal about their inductive biases and linguistic representations?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, indicating a shared inductive bias. The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional, meaning that overall performance predicts which linguistic generalizations have been acquired.
papers.conclusion: Studying learning trajectories is a promising approach to understand linguistic representations in NLMs, and the consistency suggests a mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2 and TransformerXL) also show similar learning trajectories when aligned by performance level.
The choice of training data has some effect but does not override the consistent ordering.
The learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar performance on individual phenomena.
Early in training, NLMs rely on local cues and resemble bag-of-words models; later they become more sensitive to structural cues.
future_direction: Consider the impact of additional factors, architectures and learning phases that appear only later in training.
Develop a theory that can account for the patterns presented by NLMs’ learning trajectories.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs.

papers.title: LLMs model how humans induce logically structured rules
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) model human induction of logically structured rules? Do they provide a good fit to human behavior and do they use similar logical or logic-like operators?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs can model human logical rule induction as well as Bayesian probabilistic Language of Thought (pLoT) models, and they may instantiate a novel theoretical account of human logical concepts without built-in logical primitives.
papers.conclusion: LLMs provide a good model of human logical rule induction and may offer a new theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations underlying human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.
papers.key_findings:
Some LLMs (e.g., GPT4, Gemma-7b) achieve human-level accuracy on logical rule induction tasks.
When prompted to explain rules, LLMs sometimes produce rules that use logical operators similar to humans.
Tuning an LLM (Gemma-7b) on human responses yields a better fit to human learning trajectories than tuning on correct answers or than Bayesian pLoT models.
The tuned LLM's high correlation with human data is not just due to learning the rules correctly; it captures human-like learning patterns.
The tuning generalizes to held-out rules and to new rule types (e.g., minority/majority judgments).
papers.limitation:
It is hard to know what the LLM learns when tuning to human responses, and it is hard to fully eliminate the concern that the tuning process is introducing an artifact that increases fit even on withheld exemplars.
The held-out rules share components with seen rules, so generalization might not be fully compositional.
future_direction: Investigate the representations and processes LLMs use for logical rule induction.
Compare LLM-based accounts to human cognitive processes more deeply.
papers.abstract: A central goal of cognitive science is to provide a computationally explicit account of both the structure of the mind and its development: what are the primitive representational building blocks of cognition, what are the rules via which those primitives combine, and where do these primitives and rules come from in the first place? A long-standing debate concerns the adequacy of artificial neural networks as computational models that can answer these questions, in particular in domains related to abstract cognitive function, such as language and logic. This paper argues that recent advances in neural networks -- specifically, the advent of large language models (LLMs) -- represent an important shift in this debate. We test a variety of LLMs on an existing experimental paradigm used for studying the induction of rules formulated over logical concepts. Across four experiments, we find converging empirical evidence that LLMs provide at least as good a fit to human behavior as models that implement a Bayesian probablistic language of thought (pLoT), which have been the best computational models of human behavior on the same task. Moreover, we show that the LLMs make qualitatively different predictions about the nature of the rules that are inferred and deployed in order to complete the task, indicating that the LLM is unlikely to be a mere implementation of the pLoT solution. Based on these results, we argue that LLMs may instantiate a novel theoretical account of the primitive representations and computations necessary to explain human logical concepts, with which future work in cognitive science should engage.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Levels of Analysis for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can methods from cognitive science, particularly David Marr's levels of analysis, be used to understand large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for understanding large language models by applying David Marr's three levels of analysis (computational, algorithmic, implementation) from cognitive science, and surveys established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the levels of analysis framework and the toolkit of cognitive science methods provide a valuable approach for understanding the behavior and internal organization of large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models exhibit 'embers of autoregression'—behavioral trends that reflect their next-token prediction training objective, even in deterministic tasks.
LLMs show systematic deviations from normative benchmarks such as the axioms of probability theory, similar to human biases.
Methods from cognitive psychology, such as adapted implicit association tests, can reveal hidden associations in value-aligned LLMs that are not apparent in direct questioning.
At the implementation level, techniques like activation patching and circuit discovery can identify causal mechanisms within the model's architecture.
The levels of analysis framework provides a structured toolkit for making sense of LLMs by connecting their function, algorithms, and physical implementation.
papers.abstract: Modern artificial intelligence systems, such as large language models, are increasingly powerful but also increasingly hard to understand. Recognizing this problem as analogous to the historical difficulties in understanding the human mind, we argue that methods developed in cognitive science can be useful for understanding large language models. We propose a framework for applying these methods based on the levels of analysis that David Marr proposed for studying information processing systems. By revisiting established cognitive science techniques relevant to each level and illustrating their potential to yield insights into the behavior and internal organization of large language models, we aim to provide a toolkit for making sense of these new kinds of minds.

papers.title: Math Neurosurgery: Isolating Language Models' Math Reasoning Abilities Using Only Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How is math reasoning encoded in LLM parameters, and can math-specific parameters be isolated to improve math performance without affecting general language abilities?
papers.core_contribution: MathNeuro is a method to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes; pruning these parameters deletes math ability without affecting general language, and scaling them improves math performance by 4-35%.
papers.conclusion: MathNeuro successfully isolates math-specific parameters, enabling targeted interventions to enhance math reasoning without compromising other abilities.
papers.key_findings:
MathNeuro isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out parameters important for general language tasks.
Pruning MathNeuro-identified parameters destroys math reasoning ability with minimal impact on non-math tasks.
Scaling these parameters improves math performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH.
MathNeuro is data-efficient, effective even with a single sample.
Math-specific parameters are distributed throughout decoder blocks, not concentrated in specific layers.
future_direction: Applying MathNeuro to other skills or domains
Investigating the impact of different non-math datasets
Studying the theoretical underpinnings
papers.abstract: Math reasoning is an active area of Large Language Model (LLM) research because it is a hallmark of artificial intelligence and has implications in several domains, including math education. However, few works have explored how math reasoning is encoded within LLM parameters and if it is a skill that can be isolated within models. Doing so could allow targeted intervention to improve math performance without altering non-math behavior and foster understanding of how models encode math reasoning. We introduce Math Neurosurgery (MathNeuro), a computationally efficient method we use to isolate math-specific parameters in LLMs using only forward passes. MathNeuro builds on existing work by using weights and activations to calculate parameter importance, but isolates math-specific parameters by filtering out those important for general language tasks. Through pruning parameters MathNeuro identifies, we delete a LLM's math reasoning ability without significantly impacting its general language ability. Scaling the identified parameters by a small constant improves a pretrained or instruction-tuned LLM's performance by 4-17% on GSM8K and 5-35% on MATH while leaving non-math behavior unaltered. MathNeuro is also data efficient: most of its effectiveness holds when identifying math-specific parameters using a single sample. MathNeuro highlights the potential for future work to intervene on math-specific parameters.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
papers.research_question: How can polysemantic interference structures in language models be exploited to manipulate model outputs, and do these interference patterns transfer across models of different scales and families?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that polysemantic interference structures in language models create a systematic vulnerability, and that interventions based on these structures, identified in small models, can transfer to larger instruction-tuned models for predictable behavioral control without requiring access to their internals.
papers.conclusion: Polysemantic interference reveals a systematic vulnerability in language models, and the generalization of these structures across scale and family challenges the view of polysemanticity as purely stochastic, offering new avenues for black-box control and theoretical insight into internal representation.
papers.key_findings:
Interventions leveraging polysemantic structures (feature-direction steering, token-gradient steering, prompt injection) can effectively manipulate model next-token predictions.
Polysemantic interference patterns are persistent across models: interventions distilled from small models (Pythia-70M, GPT-2-Small) transfer reliably to larger models (Llama-3.1, Gemma-2).
Many counterintuitive interference patterns are stable across models but remain largely opaque to human interpretation, suggesting models learn robust regularities not aligned with surface semantics.
Highly polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable to interventions; amplifying 'super-neurons' (activated by many features) strongly alters model behavior, while deactivating them has a reduced effect.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on sparse autoencoders (SAEs) whose outputs fluctuate with dimensionality and hyperparameters, yielding unstable features.
Interventions steer only one interference feature in one layer, while multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations could amplify and better obscure the effect.
Vulnerability is quantified solely via shifts in immediate next-token probabilities on two small base models, with only coarse transfer checks on larger instructed models.
future_direction: Establishing how these interventions alter non-trivial downstream tasks in bigger models.
Exploring multi-feature, cross-layer manipulations to amplify and better obscure intervention effects.
papers.abstract: Polysemanticity is pervasive in language models and remains a major challenge for interpretation and model behavioral control. Leveraging sparse autoencoders (SAEs), we map the polysemantic topology of two small models (Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small) to identify SAE feature pairs that are semantically unrelated yet exhibit interference within models. We intervene at four loci (prompt, token, feature, neuron) and measure induced shifts in the next-token prediction distribution, uncovering polysemantic structures that expose a systematic vulnerability in these models. Critically, interventions distilled from counterintuitive interference patterns shared by two small models transfer reliably to larger instruction-tuned models (Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct), yielding predictable behavioral shifts without access to model internals. These findings challenge the view that polysemanticity is purely stochastic, demonstrating instead that interference structures generalize across scale and family. Such generalization suggests a convergent, higher-order organization of internal representations, which is only weakly aligned with intuition and structured by latent regularities, offering new possibilities for both black-box control and theoretical insight into human and artificial cognition.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head
papers.research_question: What is the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small across the entire training distribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and explains the copy suppression mechanism of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small, showing it suppresses naive copying to improve calibration and accounts for 76.9% of the head's impact.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces copy suppression as the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small and verifies it mechanistically using weights-based analysis of QK and OV circuits, providing a comprehensive explanation of a component in a language model.
papers.key_findings:
The main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small is copy suppression, which explains 76.9% of its behavior on the training distribution.
Copy suppression reduces model loss and improves calibration by suppressing incorrect token predictions that appear earlier in context.
Copy suppression is a mechanism for self-repair, explaining 39% of self-repair in the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
The OV circuit of L10H7 suppresses the tokens it attends to, with 84.70% of tokens having their diagonal as one of the top 10 most negative values.
The QK circuit of L10H7 attends to tokens that are predicted at the query position, with 95.72% of diagonal values being the largest in their rows.
papers.limitation:
The idealised setup for analyzing the QK circuit does not completely faithfully represent L10H7's real functioning.
Using KL divergence as an ablation metric has limitations, as discussed in Appendix J.
papers.abstract: We present a single attention head in GPT-2 Small that has one main role across the entire training distribution.
